# Synthetic teaching note: eta-shrinkage and EBE-based diagnostics

This note is a synthetic fixture written for the PharmAgent test suite. It is not
taken from any book or paper; it paraphrases widely taught ideas in plain words so
that retrieval and quote-grounding can be tested without copyrighted text.

## 1 What shrinkage is

In a nonlinear mixed-effects model each subject receives an empirical Bayes
estimate (EBE) of its random effect, often called an eta. When the data for a
subject are sparse or uninformative about a parameter, the EBE is pulled toward
the population typical value. The spread of the EBEs is then smaller than the
estimated population variance omega. Eta-shrinkage quantifies this: it is one minus
the ratio of the standard deviation of the EBEs to the square root of the estimated
omega, usually expressed as a percentage.

## 2 Why it matters for diagnostics

When eta-shrinkage exceeds 30 percent, individual parameter estimates are drawn
toward the population mean and EBE-based diagnostics lose their power to reveal
model misspecification. Plots of eta against a covariate can then hide a true
relationship or suggest a false one, and individual predictions can look better
than the model deserves. Covariate screening on shrunken EBEs is therefore
uninformative and should not be used to accept or reject a covariate effect.

## 3 What to do instead

With high shrinkage, prefer diagnostics that do not depend on the EBEs: a
visual predictive check, conditional weighted residuals, or a formal covariate
test inside the estimation rather than a post-hoc regression on the etas. Report
the shrinkage for every random effect alongside the estimates so a reader can judge
which individual-level conclusions are supported by the design.

## 4 Epsilon-shrinkage

A related quantity, epsilon-shrinkage, is one minus the standard deviation of the
individual weighted residuals. High epsilon-shrinkage means the model is
over-fitting individual observations, and individual predictions will track the
data too closely to be diagnostic.
